extracted.intended_audience: pipeline operators, industry trade associations, regulators, public safety stakeholders, and other participants in PHMSA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria from PHMSA's final rule preamble establishing requirements and standards for automatic/remote-controlled/remote-monitorable valves (RMVs/ASVs/RCVs), leak detection systems, rupture identification, valve spacing, post-incident review, applicability, and related operator obligations for newly constructed and entirely replaced onshore pipelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic and Remote-Controlled Shut-Off Valves Requirement (Section 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 4 of the 2011 Pipeline Safety Act directs the Secretary, if appropriate, to require by regulation the use of ASVs or RCVs, or equivalent technology, where it is economically, technically, and operationally feasible, on hazardous liquid and gas transmission pipeline facilities that are constructed or entirely replaced after the date on which the Secretary issues the final rule containing such requirements. This final rule establishes minimum standards for the installation of RMVs or alternative equivalent technology on specified newly constructed or entirely replaced, onshore pipelines that have diameters of 6 inches or greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to newly constructed and entirely replaced onshore pipelines ≥6 inches; decision to require ASVs/RCVs depends on economic, technical, and operational feasibility. Implementation includes specifications for monitoring and control capability, spacing, and exceptions described elsewhere in the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Valve spacing limits for Class 3 and Class 4 locations
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA requires the installation of RMVs, or equivalent alternative technologies, at intervals of no more than 8 miles in Class 4 locations and 15 miles in Class 3 locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spacing requirements are informed by NTSB recommendations and risk analysis; NTSB had recommended valve spacing be based on risk analysis. The rule also contemplates site-specific risk considerations and exceptions where risk is low (e.g., PIR exceptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: RMV and alternative technology controllability and monitorability
rubrics_metrics.description: RMVs and alternative equivalent technologies must be capable of having their status controlled or monitored (directly, or indirectly via the upstream pressure, and the downstream pressure) remotely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA also requires equipment or means to monitor valve status, commodity pressures, and flow rates to support rupture detection and isolation. This monitoring can be integrated into leak detection systems and must be reliable and continuous for RCV operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rupture identification and confirmation criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule requires operators to confirm that a rupture is occurring following any one of the criteria specified in a new regulatory definition for the 'notification of [a] potential rupture.' The NPRM proposed a 10-minute rupture identification threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirement to confirm a rupture addresses concerns that operators may ignore alarms, restart pumps, or open valves during large releases. Operators must adopt procedures that use specified criteria to determine whether a potential rupture has occurred before taking further actions or notifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: RMV closure / pipeline segment isolation time objective (NPRM proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the NPRM PHMSA proposed establishing a 40-minute maximum RMV closure time and a 10-minute rupture identification threshold to shorten pipeline segment isolation times in response to rupture events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 40-minute closure objective and 10-minute detection threshold were proposed to reduce the amount of commodity released and mitigate consequences (e.g., fires, environmental damage). Related studies cited evidence that for some hazardous liquid scenarios isolation within 15 minutes provides significant mitigation; site-specific feasibility and technical limits must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-event review and failure investigation requirements (§§192.617 and 195.402)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule includes specific post-event review requirements in §§192.617 and 195.402. Operators must make those post-event reviews available for PHMSA to inspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-event reviews are intended to help operators determine system-wide lessons learned, incorporate findings into training and procedures, and inform PHMSA in future rulemakings and guidance documents. They support continuous improvement of incident response and mitigation practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency response plan updates and 9-1-1 notification
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule requires operators of all gas and hazardous liquid pipelines subject to the emergency planning requirements at §§192.615 and 195.402, respectively, to update their emergency response plans to provide for immediate and direct notification of appropriate public safety answering points (9-1-1 emergency call centers) following the notification of a potential rupture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate, direct 9-1-1 notification aims to reduce delays in emergency response and address situations where pipeline operators may not be the first to detect a rupture (e.g., residents discovering releases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Leak Detection Systems (LDS) capability study and standards (Section 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 8 of the 2011 Pipeline Safety Act required a report on LDSs and to establish technically, operationally, and economically feasible standards for the capability of LDSs to detect leaks. PHMSA commissioned a leak detection study that assessed technologies, limitations, operational practices, cost-benefit, and industry standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study tasks included assessing past incidents, reviewing technologies and retrofit potential, studying operational practices, performing cost-benefit analyses, and examining standards/regulations. PHMSA used the study to require pressure/flow monitoring related to RMVs and continues rulemaking (RIN 2137-AF51) to set minimum performance standards for LDS programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability to gathering pipelines and class distinctions (Type A/B/C)
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRM intended RMV requirements to apply to new and entirely replaced regulated gathering pipelines; in the final rule PHMSA narrowed valve installation requirements to Type A gas gathering pipelines only. Type B and Type C gas gathering pipelines are exempted. An exception is provided if a rupture on a new or entirely replaced Type A gas gathering pipeline in Class 2 locations would yield a PIR of 150 feet or less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA based the scope decision on distinguishable risk profiles: Type A lines operate at higher pressures and in higher population density areas, warranting RMVs; Type B/C operate at lower pressures and present lower PIR risk. PHMSA will gather additional data for future consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with existing leak detection and patrol requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA notes existing regulatory requirements: hazardous liquid operators have been required since 2002 to evaluate and install LDS in HCAs; 2019 regulations require hazardous liquid pipelines outside HCAs to have an effective leak detection system; distribution and transmission patrol and leak survey requirements apply per §§192.722, 192.723, 192.705, and 192.706.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA expects pressure monitoring required by this rule to be integrated into current and future LDS and analyses. Operators must continue patrols/leak surveys at statutorily required intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity management risk analysis obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Operators of existing pipelines are required under the integrity management (IM) regulations at §§192.935 and 195.452 to conduct risk analyses to identify measures (including installing ASVs, RCVs, or EFRDs) as appropriate to enhance safety on pipeline segments that are in or could affect HCAs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA indicates that expanding the new valve-installation requirements to existing pipelines would be beyond the NPRM scope and could have environmental downsides (e.g., blowdowns), but IM risk analyses remain the mechanism for identifying needed mitigations on existing systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic, technical, and operational feasibility considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: PHMSA and commissioned studies evaluated whether installing ASVs and RCVs is technically, operationally, and economically feasible on newly constructed and entirely replaced pipelines, finding general feasibility given space for valve bodies/actuators/power/sensors and reliable communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies concluded benefits would exceed costs for certain release scenarios but cautioned site-specific variables must be considered. Commenters challenged PHMSA's cost estimates; PHMSA must make a reasoned determination that benefits justify costs when proposing standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance-based incident response goals and data improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: GAO recommended improving the reliability of incident response data and using it to evaluate whether to implement a performance-based framework for incident response times. GAO suggested defined performance-based goals could improve operator response and that ASV/RCV installation/use is one factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA agrees that more precise performance-based standards, paired with carefully selected requirements, could better improve incident response times. Reliable data and sound agency assessments are prerequisites for performance-based goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operator procedural anti-patterns to avoid (ignoring alarms, restarting pumps)
rubrics_metrics.description: The leak detection study noted that operator procedures may have allowed ignoring alarms, restarting pumps, or opening valves during large releases, which can delay or prevent proper response to large releases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA addresses these anti-patterns by requiring confirmation criteria for potential ruptures, post-incident reviews, and updates to training and procedures to ensure alarms and automated indicators are acted upon appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance for alternative equivalent technologies
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule permits installation of RMVs or 'equivalent alternative technologies' in lieu of RMVs, provided they meet the objectives for monitoring, control capability, and isolation performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives must be functionally equivalent (e.g., remote control/monitoring, pressure/flow monitoring, isolation capability). Operators may use risk analysis and site-specific assessments to justify equivalent approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-benefit and economic impact considerations in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters argued PHMSA's Preliminary Regulatory Impact Assessment understated costs; PHMSA must support the rule with a reasoned determination that benefits justify costs. PHMSA considered potential environmental harms (e.g., blowdowns) if applied to existing pipelines and balanced cost estimates and differing stakeholder views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA considered public comments questioning cost estimates and provided rationale for scope decisions. Some stakeholders argued implementation costs should be treated as standard construction/repair costs rather than 'extra' infrastructure; PHMSA weighed these perspectives in finalizing scope and requirements.
